findings.summary: backdate_client sets up state with raw SQL against the `oidc_client` table and its `created`/`last_modified` columns, which ties the tests to the private database schema instead of the public API.
findings.failure_scenario: Renaming the table or columns, or changing them to `timestamptz`, breaks every test in the file at setup (a SQL error, or asyncpg rejecting a naive datetime) even though the HTTP behaviour still works. This is setup, not the check, and tests/handlers/oidc_test.py:1121 already uses the same pattern, so it is acceptable. It also makes the PATCH-time assertions observable without a sleep.

findings.summary: In test_patch_by_other_admin_records_modifier, the `last_modified` check only asserts the value is not the backdated string, so any other value passes, including a wrong time or a later timestamp with a fractional part.
findings.failure_scenario: If an update set `last_modified` to some fixed or garbage time other than 2020-01-01T12:00:00Z, this test would still pass. test_patch_last_modified_is_time_of_update (line 188) and the cookie and creator tests bound the value between `before` and `after`, so the criterion is still covered. The weak assertion only matters if this test is read on its own.

findings.summary: The only PATCH on a client that is not backdated (created and patched in the same second) checks the timestamp format only. It never checks that `last_modified >= created` or that `created` is unchanged in that case.
findings.failure_scenario: The contract says `last_modified` may equal `created` but is never before it when both fall in the same second. An implementation that truncated the update time differently from the creation time (for example, rounding `created` up), producing last_modified < created within one second, would pass every test, because the other PATCH tests compare against the backdated 2020 `created`.
